title: Credentials from Password Stores: Password Managers
shortTitle: Credentials from Password Stores: Password Managers
summary: Third-party password managers hold a user's entire credential set inside one encrypted database that is unlocked with a master password. While the vault is open, the plaintext entries and often the derived master key exist in the process memory, because the application needs them to fill forms and copy secrets to the clipboard. Attackers therefore rarely attack the file encryption directly. They read the memory of the running password manager, inject code into it, or abuse a documented software flaw that makes it export or reveal entries without the master password. A second path is guessing the master password once a copy of the vault file has been taken, which succeeds when the master password is short or reused elsewhere. The on-disk artefact is a vault file with an unusual extension inside the user profile, sometimes duplicated into a temporary directory or an archive. The in-memory artefact is a process handle with read or write rights opened against the manager, or an unexpected module loaded into it. Normal use looks like the same process reading its own memory, so the differentiators are who opened the handle and whether the vault file was copied.

beginner.definition: A password manager is an application that keeps all your passwords in one encrypted file. You open that file with a single master password. This technique means an attacker steals the passwords from the manager, usually while it is unlocked and running.
beginner.whyItMatters: One password manager holds everything: email, work accounts, banking, and shared team logins. If an attacker reads it, they do not need to guess anything else. The master password alone protects the whole vault, so a weak or reused one fails quickly during offline guessing. Ignoring this risk turns a single unlocked laptop into a complete identity theft.
howItWorks: The password manager stores every login in one encrypted database file on your disk.
You type a master password, and the application uses it to unlock the whole database.
While the vault is open, the readable passwords sit in the memory of that program.
An attacker reads that memory or injects code to pull the passwords out.
Another route is copying the database file and guessing the master password offline.
Some attackers abuse a software bug that makes the manager reveal or export its entries.
beginner.example: Picture an office safe that holds every key in the building. The safe is strong and its combination is long. The staff open it in the morning and leave it open all day, because they need keys many times. A visitor who reaches the office simply takes what is inside, because the door is already standing open. Even a visitor who comes at night can photograph the safe. At home they can try combinations, where nobody watches and nothing locks them out.
takeaways: An open password manager keeps plaintext secrets in memory, so endpoint visibility matters.
Look for processes opening handles to password manager programs or copying vault files.
A long, unique master password is the main defence if the vault file is stolen.

objectives: Explain how a password manager stores and unlocks credentials.
Describe why running memory, rather than the encrypted file, is the usual target.
Identify host telemetry that shows a vault file copied or a process memory read.
Explain at a high level how offline guessing against a stolen vault works.
Advise users on master password strength and on locking the vault when idle.
